a: the Jews were trying to kill him
p: Everyone in this story is Jewish, Jesus included. Here the word points to the Jerusalem authorities.
b: The Greek hoi Ioudaioi can mean the Jewish people, the people of Judea ("Judeans"), or, as often in John, the Jerusalem leaders who oppose Jesus. In this verse Jesus avoids Judea because "the Jews" want him dead, which looks back to 5:18, where the people angered by his Sabbath healing were the temple authorities, not the whole nation. The Plain English Translation keeps the word John wrote, as most English Bibles do, and these notes say each time who seems to be meant. In chapters 7–10 the same word covers hostile leaders (7:13; 9:22), a puzzled crowd (7:35), people who believe (8:31; compare 11:45), and a divided audience (10:19). See the topic page for the full debate and the later misuse of these chapters against Jews.

a: the Feast of Booths
p: Sukkot, the autumn harvest festival, when Israel lived in shelters for a week and remembered the wilderness.
b: Skēnopēgia, "shelter-pitching," is the Greek name for Sukkot. Older English Bibles call it the Feast of Tabernacles; this site, like many modern Bibles, says "Feast of Booths", as in Leviticus 23:34. A sukkah is a simple shelter of branches. It came in September or October, after the grape and olive harvest. The law says, "Live in booths for seven days" (Leviticus 23:42), to recall the wilderness years, and adds an eighth day of closing assembly (Leviticus 23:36). Josephus calls it the holiest and greatest festival of the Jews (Antiquities 8.100). In Jesus' day it drew huge crowds of pilgrims, and the Mishnah describes two famous temple rites: water drawn from the pool of Siloam and poured on the altar each morning, and giant lamps lit in the Court of Women at night. Both lie behind what Jesus says in 7:37–39 and 8:12. Zechariah 14:16–19 pictured all nations coming up to keep this festival.

a: his brothers
p: His brothers doubt him now but appear among the believers after Easter. Churches differ on who they were.
b: The Gospels name four brothers, James, Joses (Joseph), Judas and Simon, and mention sisters (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55). Here they speak like managers: a miracle worker should perform in the capital. John adds bluntly that they did not believe (7:5). Yet after the resurrection they pray with the disciples (Acts 1:14), the risen Jesus appears to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and James leads the Jerusalem church (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13). Whether they were younger sons of Mary, sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or cousins is one of the old questions between churches; see the card on this chapter's page.
r: Mark 3:21; Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55; Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:7; Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13

a: The right moment for me
p: Jesus uses kairos, the right or fitting moment, not the clock time his brothers think in.
b: Kairos is a time that is ripe for something: an opportunity, a season, a fitting moment. Jesus' brothers can go any time, because nothing hangs on their timing. His timing belongs to the Father. Elsewhere John speaks of Jesus' "hour" (hōra), the hour of his death and glory (2:4; 7:30; 8:20; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). The two words are close here: the brothers want Jesus to show himself at the festival, and the moment when he will truly be shown to the world is the cross, at a later Passover. The same pattern comes in 2:4, where he first refuses and then acts quietly.
orig: ὁ καιρὸς ὁ ἐμὸς (ho kairos ho emos), 'my right time'

a: I am not going up to this festival
p: He says he is not going, then goes. Some copyists changed "not" to "not yet"; readers have explained it several ways.
b: The oldest form of the saying is probably "I am not going up"; many manuscripts soften it to "not yet" (see the variant). The pagan critic Porphyry (about AD 270) used this verse to charge Jesus with changing his mind, as Jerome reports. Readers answer in several ways: (1) Jesus refuses to go as his brothers ask, publicly, as a pilgrim leading a show, and then goes quietly (7:10); (2) "go up" carries a double meaning in John, since Jesus will "go up" to the Father (20:17), and that going up is not at this festival; (3) as at Cana (2:4–7), he refuses human pressure and then acts at the Father's prompting. All three keep the point that his steps are set by the Father, not by family.

a: the Jews kept searching for him
p: Probably the Jerusalem authorities, as in 7:1. The crowds in 7:12–13 are afraid of them.
b: The people looking for Jesus are set apart from "the crowds" in the next verse, who whisper because they fear "the Jews" (7:13). Since the crowds are Jewish too, the word here must mean a smaller group: the leaders in Jerusalem who already want Jesus dead (7:1; 5:18). Some scholars translate "the Judeans" in such places, to mark people of Judea against Galileans; most keep "the Jews" and explain it. See the note at 7:1.

a: he is misleading the crowd
p: The charge of a false teacher who leads Israel away from God, later repeated in Jewish and pagan sources.
b: Planaō means to lead someone off the road, to deceive. Deuteronomy 13 orders death for a prophet who works signs but leads Israel away from God, and the debate in John 7–10 circles around that law: are Jesus' signs from God (9:16, 33; 10:21) or a trap? The same charge appears in Matthew 27:63 ("that deceiver"), in Justin Martyr's report that Jews called Jesus "a magician and a deceiver of the people" (Dialogue with Trypho 69), and in a later passage of the Babylonian Talmud that says Yeshu "practiced sorcery and led Israel astray" (Sanhedrin 43a). The Pharisees ask the officers in 7:47, using the same verb, whether they too have been misled.

a: because they were afraid of the Jews
p: The crowd is Jewish too, so "the Jews" here must mean those with power in Jerusalem.
b: The people who whisper in the crowd are themselves Jewish pilgrims and Jerusalemites. When John says they fear "the Jews," he plainly means the authorities, the chief priests and their allies, who could punish them. The same phrase returns for the blind man's parents (9:22), for Joseph of Arimathea (19:38) and for the disciples behind locked doors (20:19). Translations such as the NIV and NRSVue write "the Jewish leaders" or "the Jewish authorities" in places like this to stop readers from hearing a whole people. This site keeps John's word, as the Greek has it, and makes the point here instead.

a: went up to the temple and started teaching
p: "The temple" here is the great outer complex, where teachers gathered crowds in the porches.
b: John uses hieron, the whole temple complex, not naos, the sanctuary building only priests entered. Herod's rebuilt temple sat on a platform of about 35 acres, ringed with colonnades where teachers sat with their students (compare Luke 2:46; Acts 5:12). Jesus arrives halfway through the eight days, about the fourth day, when the city was at its fullest. His teaching from here to 8:59 takes place in these courts, and each saying ties to something visible there: the water rite (7:37–38), the lamps and the treasury in the Court of Women (8:12, 20), and at the end Solomon's Porch (10:23).

a: He has never been anyone's student
p: Literally "How does he know letters, never having learned?" The point is formal training, not reading ability.
b: Grammata, "letters," can mean the alphabet, writings, or learning in the Scriptures. "Never having learned" (mē memathēkōs) means he had not studied under a recognized teacher, the way a student sat with a rabbi or a scribe. Compare Acts 4:13, where Peter and John are "unlettered" men. So the question is likely "Where did he get his learning?" rather than "How can he read?" Jesus answers that his teacher is the one who sent him (7:16). Chris Keith argues that this verse and 8:6 show early Christians debating whether Jesus belonged to the scribal class at all.
orig: Πῶς οὗτος γράμματα οἶδεν μὴ μεμαθηκώς; (pōs houtos grammata oiden mē memathēkōs)

a: I did a single work
p: Jesus means the Sabbath healing at the pool of Bethesda in chapter 5, still a live issue.
b: The "single work" is the healing of the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, done on a Sabbath (5:1–18). The argument it started, about Sabbath and about Jesus calling God his own Father, is picked up again here months later. Some scholars think chapters 5 and 7 once stood next to each other and that chapter 6 was moved; others see John deliberately bringing an old quarrel back at a new festival. Either way the debate in chapter 7 continues the trial that began at Bethesda: "Why are you out to kill me?" (7:19) echoes 5:18.

a: not that it comes from Moses; it comes from the ancestors
p: Circumcision began with Abraham, generations before the law of Moses.
b: God gave circumcision to Abraham as the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:10–14), and the law of Moses then set it on the eighth day: "On the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin is to be circumcised" (Leviticus 12:3). Jesus' aside matters for the argument. Circumcision is older than the Sabbath law given through Moses, so when the eighth day falls on a Sabbath, the older command wins. Paul uses a similar point about Abraham's faith coming before the law (Romans 4:9–12; Galatians 3:17).

a: That is why
p: The Greek words can end 7:21 ("you are all astonished at it") or begin 7:22, as the Plain English Translation takes them.
b: Dia touto means "because of this, that is why." The oldest manuscripts have no punctuation, so editors must decide. SBL and NA28 put the words at the start of 7:22: Moses gave circumcision for this reason, that is, to show that a command can override the Sabbath. Many older interpreters, and some manuscripts and versions, attach them to 7:21: "all of you are astonished because of it," which is smoother Greek but makes John use the phrase in an unusual way. The Plain English Translation follows the SBL punctuation. Either way, the argument that follows is the same.
orig: διὰ τοῦτο (dia touto)

a: are you furious with me for making a whole man healthy on the Sabbath
p: Jewish law already let circumcision override the Sabbath. Jesus argues from the smaller case to the greater.
b: The Mishnah says that everything needed for a circumcision may be done on the Sabbath (Shabbat 18:3; 19:2), and "circumcision overrides the Sabbath" was a known rule. Jesus argues in a form the rabbis called qal vahomer, "light and heavy": if repairing one part of the body is allowed on the Sabbath, how much more making the whole person well. Later rabbis used almost the same argument to allow saving a life on the Sabbath: "If circumcision, which concerns one of a person's limbs, overrides the Sabbath, how much more the whole body" (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b, in the name of Rabbi Eleazar). This shows Jesus arguing inside Jewish legal reasoning, not against the law.

a: Do not judge by how things look on the surface
p: The law told judges to judge justly, not by appearances or by who someone is.
b: Kat' opsin, "by sight, by appearance," echoes the old instructions to Israel's judges: "Judge your fellow citizen in what is right" (Leviticus 19:15), and do not show favor (Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 16:18–19). The LORD told Samuel that people look at the outside but God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7), and Isaiah promised a king who would not judge by what his eyes see (Isaiah 11:3). Jesus turns the law on his judges. The whole section is a trial, and the reader is asked to judge too.

a: no one knows where he is from
p: Some Jews expected the Messiah to appear suddenly, from an unknown origin.
b: Jewish expectations about the Messiah were not uniform. One strand held that he would be hidden until God revealed him. Justin Martyr's Jewish partner Trypho says the Messiah, if he has been born, "is unknown and does not even know himself" until Elijah anoints him (Dialogue with Trypho 8). In 1 Enoch the Son of Man was "hidden" before creation (1 Enoch 48:6), and 4 Ezra 13:52 says no one can see God's Son until his day comes. Another strand expected a son of David from Bethlehem (7:42). John's irony is that the crowd thinks it knows Jesus' origin (Nazareth), while the reader knows he comes "from above" (8:23).

a: So you know me, and you know where I come from?
p: The Greek has no punctuation. Jesus may agree, ask, or speak with sharp irony.
b: Kame oidate kai oidate pothen eimi can be read as a statement ("Yes, you know me and where I am from"), as a question ("Do you know me?"), or as irony ("So you know me, do you?"). Ancient manuscripts had no question marks, so editors choose. Most commentators hear irony, because Jesus at once says they do not know the one who sent him. They know his hometown and family, but not his true origin. The Plain English Translation uses a question to let the irony show.
orig: Κἀμὲ οἴδατε καὶ οἴδατε πόθεν εἰμί (kame oidate kai oidate pothen eimi)

a: his hour had still not come
p: John's clock: no one can stop Jesus until the Father's hour, the hour of the cross.
b: From Cana onward John marks Jesus' "hour" (2:4). Attempts to seize or kill him fail "because his hour had not yet come" (7:30; 8:20), and he slips away (8:59; 10:39). Then, after Greeks ask to see him, he says, "The hour is here when the Son of Man will be glorified" (12:23), and the passion begins (13:1; 17:1). The refrain tells the first readers, who knew how the story ended, that Jesus' death was not an accident of politics but a time set by God.

a: guards
p: The guards were the temple police under the chief priests, not Roman soldiers.
b: Hypēretai, "assistants, attendants," were the Levite guards and officials who kept order in the temple under the high priest and the captain of the temple (Acts 4:1; 5:24–26). The "chief priests" were the high priest and the leading priestly families. John pairs them with the Pharisees as the council that ruled Jerusalem's religious life (11:47, 57; 18:3). Historically the priests, not the Pharisees, controlled the guard; John's phrase names the alliance that opposed Jesus as his own readers remembered it, since after AD 70 the Pharisees' heirs led Jewish life.

a: the Dispersion in the Greek world
p: Jews living outside the land of Israel. John's readers knew the good news did go to Greeks.
b: Diaspora, "scattering," meant the Jews living abroad, from Babylon to Rome, who far outnumbered those in Judea. "The Dispersion of the Greeks" probably means the Jews scattered in the Greek-speaking world; "to teach the Greeks" may mean Gentiles. The mockers say more than they know. Within a few years the message about Jesus was taught in the synagogues of the Dispersion and then to Gentiles (Acts 11:19–20), and in John Greeks come to see Jesus just as his hour arrives (12:20–23). John's own readers, perhaps in Ephesus, were the proof.

a: its last and great day
p: Each morning of the festival, priests poured water from Siloam on the altar. Jesus speaks into that rite.
b: The Mishnah describes a procession that went down to the pool of Siloam each morning of the festival, filled a golden pitcher, and brought the water up to the altar to the sound of trumpets, where it was poured out with the wine offering (Sukkah 4:9). It says, "Whoever has not seen the joy of the water-drawing has never seen joy in his life" (Sukkah 5:1). The rite prayed for the winter rains and was linked to Isaiah 12:3: "You will draw water with joy out of the springs of rescue" (Isaiah 12:3). "The last and great day" is either the seventh day, when the altar was circled seven times, or the eighth day of assembly (Leviticus 23:36). On that day Jesus offers himself as the source of the water.

a: The one who believes in me
t: Whose belly? Two ways to punctuate
p: The rivers may flow from the believer or from Jesus himself, depending on where the sentence breaks.
b: Ancient Greek had no punctuation, and 7:37–38 can be divided two ways. (1) "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. The one who believes in me, as Scripture says, out of his belly rivers will flow." The rivers flow from the believer, who becomes a spring for others (compare 4:14). Origen and most Greek fathers read it so, and so does this Plain English Translation. (2) "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me; and let the one who believes in me drink. As Scripture says, out of his belly rivers will flow." Then the rivers flow from Jesus, as water and blood flow from his side on the cross (19:34). Some early Latin writers and many modern scholars, such as Raymond Brown, favor this.
orig: ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμέ (ho pisteuōn eis eme)

a: as the Scripture has said
p: No verse says this word for word. John points to a cluster of prophecies about water from God's house.
b: Several passages may stand behind it. Zechariah 14:8 promises living waters flowing out from Jerusalem, and the Talmud says Zechariah 14 was read at this festival (Megillah 31a). Ezekiel 47:1–12 sees a river flowing from the temple, growing deeper and healing the Dead Sea. In the wilderness God gave water from the rock: "He drew running streams from a crag and sent water down like rivers" (Psalm 78:16; compare Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11), and Paul says that rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Isaiah 58:11 says the faithful will be like a spring that never fails, and Isaiah 44:3 links water with God's Spirit, as 7:39 does.
r: Zechariah 14:8; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Psalm 78:16; Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11; Isaiah 44:3; Isaiah 58:11; Joel 3:18; 1 Corinthians 10:4; Revelation 22:1–2

a: Out of his belly
p: Greek koilia, the inside of a person. Many versions say "heart"; the bodily word is kept here.
b: Koilia means belly, womb, the inner parts. In Hebrew thought the inner parts were the seat of feeling and of the inner self, so versions often turn it into "heart" or "from within." The Plain English Translation keeps John's bodily word, because it may link to the body of Jesus, from whose side water flows (19:34), and because "living water" itself is a concrete image: fresh, running water, as opposed to still water in a cistern. In 4:10–14 Jesus used the same image with the Samaritan woman.
orig: ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας αὐτοῦ (ek tēs koilias autou), 'out of his belly'

a: For the Spirit had not yet come
p: Literally "the Spirit was not yet." John does not mean the Spirit did not exist, but had not yet been given.
b: The Greek is short and startling: oupō gar ēn pneuma, "for the Spirit was not yet." The Spirit was active in creation (Genesis 1:2) and in the prophets, and John has already shown the Spirit resting on Jesus (1:32–33). The point is that the Spirit had not yet been poured out on believers in the way the prophets promised (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28). That gift waits for Jesus' glorifying, his death and rising, and comes in 20:22 (and in Acts 2 at Pentecost). Copyists filled the gap in different ways; see the variant.
orig: οὔπω γὰρ ἦν πνεῦμα (oupō gar ēn pneuma)

a: Jesus had not yet been glorified
p: In John, Jesus is "glorified" by being lifted up on the cross and raised.
b: Most readers expect glory to mean triumph and fame. In John, glory is God's presence shown, and it is shown most clearly in Jesus' death: "The hour is here when the Son of Man will be glorified" (12:23), said just before he speaks of a grain of wheat dying. The disciples understand some of his words only "when Jesus was glorified" (12:16). So the cross, resurrection and return to the Father are one movement of glory, and the Spirit is its fruit.

a: the Prophet
p: Moses promised that God would raise up "a prophet like me." Many expected one great Prophet at the end.
b: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers" (Deuteronomy 18:15). By Jesus' day many read this as a single figure to come. The Dead Sea Scrolls expect "a prophet and the anointed ones of Aaron and Israel" (Community Rule 9:11), and Samaritans hoped for a prophet-teacher they called the Taheb. John the Baptist denied being the Prophet (1:21), but after the feeding in the wilderness the crowd said Jesus was (6:14). Here the crowd splits between "the Prophet" and "the Messiah" (7:41), as if they were two figures. Christians came to see Jesus as both (Acts 3:22–23).

a: Bethlehem, David's home village
p: The crowd cites Micah and the promise to David. John's readers would catch the irony.
b: The Scripture they have in mind includes God's promise to David, "I will raise up your offspring to come after you" (2 Samuel 7:12), and Micah 5:2, a ruler for Israel from Bethlehem, "small among the clans of Judah." Matthew and Luke say Jesus was born in Bethlehem and was of David's line (Matthew 2:1–6; Luke 2:4–7), and Paul calls him a descendant of David (Romans 1:3). John never says so. Most interpreters hear irony: the speakers think they know Jesus' origin, and the reader knows they are wrong. A minority of critical scholars think John either did not know a Bethlehem birth or did not care about it, since for him Jesus' true origin is "from above."
r: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Micah 5:2; Psalm 89:3–4; Matthew 2:1–6; Luke 2:4–7; Romans 1:3; 1:45–46

a: they are cursed
t: "This crowd that does not know the law"
p: An elite sneer at ordinary people who could not study the law. Later rabbis knew this attitude too.
b: The speakers draw a line between experts in the law and the common people, whom later rabbinic writings call the am ha-arets, "people of the land." Hillel is quoted as saying, "An ignorant person cannot be truly pious" (Mishnah Avot 2:5). The curse may echo Deuteronomy 27:26, a curse on anyone who does not keep the law. John shows the leaders scorning the very people who are coming to believe, and then being corrected from their own ranks by Nicodemus (7:50–51). The verse shows a class divide inside Judaism, not a quarrel between Jews and Christians.

a: Nicodemus
p: The Pharisee who came to Jesus by night now speaks up for fair process, and later helps bury him.
b: Nicodemus came to Jesus at night in 3:1–21 and heard about being born from above. Here, among his fellow rulers, he does not confess faith, but he insists on a fair hearing. In 19:39 he brings about seventy-five pounds of spices for Jesus' burial. Readers have long debated whether he became a believer. John seems to show a man moving slowly from night toward light, and to warn readers like him who believed in secret for fear of being put out (12:42).

a: Our law does not judge a person unless it first hears from him
p: The law required judges to hear both sides and investigate before a verdict.
b: Deuteronomy tells judges to hear cases between brothers fairly (Deuteronomy 1:16–17) and to investigate thoroughly before punishing (Deuteronomy 17:4; 19:18). Later Jewish law surrounded capital cases with safeguards, such as requiring witnesses to be examined and allowing arguments for acquittal to be heard first (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1; 5:1–4). Nicodemus uses the leaders' own law against their haste, just after they claimed that the crowd does not know the law (7:49). Jesus himself said, "Do not judge by how things look" (7:24).

a: out of Galilee no prophet is raised up
p: Jonah came from Galilee, so the claim overstates. One early papyrus reads "the Prophet."
b: Jonah son of Amittai was "the prophet from Gath-hepher" (2 Kings 14:25), a village in Galilee a few miles from Nazareth, and later rabbis said that no tribe of Israel lacked a prophet (Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 27b). So the rulers' claim is a put-down, not a careful statement. Papyrus 66, from about AD 200, reads "the Prophet does not arise from Galilee," which would make their claim fit 7:40: the end-time Prophet like Moses would not come from there. See the variant.

a: Then they went away, each one to his own home.
p: 7:53–8:11 is missing from the oldest manuscripts. It was added to John later, but it may be an old, true story.
b: The story of the woman caught in adultery is not in the earliest Greek manuscripts of John (Papyrus 66 and 75, Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus), and no Greek church writer comments on it before Euthymius Zigabenus in the 1100s. It first appears in a Greek copy in Codex Bezae (400s), was known to Latin writers like Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine, and in some manuscripts stands after John 7:36, 7:44 or 21:25, or after Luke 21:38. Its words are more like Luke's than John's. Yet a story about Jesus and a woman accused of sins was known by the 200s in Syria (the Didascalia) and perhaps to Papias. Almost all scholars, conservative and liberal, agree it was not part of John's first text; many think it preserves a genuine early tradition. See the variant and the chapter page.

a: At daybreak he was back in the temple
p: The vocabulary of this story matches Luke's Gospel, which also has Jesus teaching at dawn in the temple.
b: Words such as orthros ("daybreak"), laos ("the people"), paraginomai ("arrive") and the phrase "the scribes and the Pharisees" (8:3) are common in Luke and rare or absent elsewhere in John. Luke 21:37–38 says Jesus spent his nights on the Mount of Olives and that all the people came early in the morning to hear him in the temple, which is exactly the setting of 7:53–8:2. That is why one family of manuscripts, the Ferrar group (family 13), places the story after Luke 21:38. Teachers sat to teach (Matthew 5:1; Luke 4:20).

a: The scribes and the Pharisees
p: This is the only place John's Gospel mentions scribes, another sign the story came from elsewhere.
b: Scribes were the experts who copied, taught and applied the law of Moses; many were Pharisees, but the groups were not the same. Matthew, Mark and Luke pair "the scribes and the Pharisees" again and again (Matthew 23; Luke 5:21; 6:7). John never does, except here. In this story they act as accusers who want to trap Jesus, as in the Synoptic disputes over taxes and divorce (Mark 12:13–17; Mark 10:2).

a: ordered us to stone women like this
t: What the law said about adultery
p: The law ordered death for both the man and the woman. Only one is brought here.
b: Leviticus says, "A man who commits adultery with another man's wife, who commits adultery with his neighbor's wife, must be put to death, the man and the woman who commit adultery" (Leviticus 20:10; compare Deuteronomy 22:22). Stoning is named for a betrothed young woman and her partner (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). The Mishnah, written down about AD 200, assigns stoning to the betrothed and strangling to a married woman (Sanhedrin 7:4; 11:1), so she may have been betrothed. Either way the law required both guilty parties and reliable witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6). The absent man is the story's loudest silence, and it shows the accusers using the law as a tool.

a: They were saying this to test him
p: If Jesus says "stone her," he may clash with Rome and his own mercy. If he says "let her go," he defies Moses.
b: John 18:31 says that under Roman rule the Jewish leaders were not allowed to put anyone to death. Whether that was true in every case is debated: A. N. Sherwin-White argued that Rome kept this power for itself, while Jean Juster and Paul Winter pointed to Stephen's stoning (Acts 7:58) and the temple warning inscription as signs that the council could still execute. If the rule held, a "yes" could put Jesus in conflict with the governor and with his reputation as a friend of sinners (Luke 7:34), and a "no" would make him a teacher against Moses. The shape is like the trap about paying taxes to Caesar (Mark 12:13–17). Jesus refuses both options and moves the question from the woman's guilt to the accusers' own.

a: began to write in the dirt with his finger
p: The story does not say. Readers have offered many guesses.
b: Proposals include: (1) a verse such as Jeremiah 17:13, "Those who turn away from me will be written in the earth," turning the accusation back on the accusers; (2) the sins of the accusers, as a few later manuscripts say in 8:8 ("the sins of each one of them"); (3) the judgment, since a Roman judge wrote out his sentence before reading it aloud (T. W. Manson's suggestion), so that the sentence Jesus then speaks is 8:7; (4) an echo of God's finger writing the law on stone (Exodus 31:18), the lawgiver now kneeling in the dust; (5) nothing in particular, a deliberate refusal to answer on their terms. Chris Keith argues the scene was meant to show that Jesus could write, against doubts like 7:15.

a: Whichever one of you has never sinned, let him throw a stone at her first
p: The law said the witnesses must throw first. Jesus adds a condition that no one can meet.
b: Deuteronomy said, "The hands of the witnesses are to be first against him to put him to death, and after that the hands of all the people" (Deuteronomy 17:7). Jesus keeps the law's order but asks who is anamartētos, "without sin." The word may mean without sin in this matter (some ancient readers thought the accusers were guilty of adultery themselves), or simply sinless. Either way the saying does not deny the law; it asks whether these judges are fit to carry it out. The line has become one of the most quoted sayings of Jesus in English.
orig: ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν (ho anamartētos hymōn), 'the sinless one among you'

a: starting with the elders
p: Presbyteroi can mean older men or the town's elders. Either way, those with most standing go first.
b: Presbyteroi means "older ones" and was also the title of community leaders, the elders. The oldest may leave first because they have lived long enough to know their sins, as early preachers liked to say, or because the leaders lead the retreat as they had led the accusation. The Textus Receptus adds "even to the last" and "convicted by their own conscience"; see the variant.
orig: ἀπὸ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων (apo tōn presbyterōn)

a: I do not condemn you either
p: Jesus refuses to condemn her and also tells her not to sin again. Readers have stressed one or the other.
b: Augustine summed up the scene: "Two were left, the wretched woman and Mercy" (Tractates on John 33.5). Jesus does not deny that she sinned; he sends her away with the same command he gave the man at Bethesda, "Do not keep on sinning" (5:14). Augustine also reports that some men removed the story from their copies, fearing it would give their wives permission to sin (On Adulterous Marriages 2.7.6), which may help explain why it is missing in so many manuscripts. Some readers today stress the warning, others the welcome; the story holds both.

a: sir
p: Kyrie is a polite "sir," but also the word Christians used for Jesus as Lord.
b: Kyrie is the ordinary polite address, "sir," and also the title "Lord." On the lips of a stranger the Plain English Translation uses "sir" (compare 4:11; 9:36), and "Lord" where a speaker confesses faith (9:38). Some readers hear more in her word, as the KJV's "Lord" allows. John often lets a character say more than she knows.
orig: κύριε (kyrie)

a: I am the light of the world
p: At the Feast of Booths huge lamps lit the temple at night. Jesus claims to be the light they pointed to.
b: The Mishnah says that on the first night of the festival four great golden lampstands were lit in the Court of Women, so high that young priests climbed ladders to fill them, and "there was no courtyard in Jerusalem that was not lit" by them. Pious men danced with torches through the night (Sukkah 5:2–4). The lights recalled the pillar of fire that lit Israel's way in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21). God himself is Israel's light: "The LORD is my light and my rescue" (Psalm 27:1), and his servant would be "a light to the nations" (Isaiah 42:6; compare Isaiah 49:6). "Follows me" fits the pillar too: Israel walked behind it. This is the second of John's seven pictured "I am" sayings; see the topic page.

a: You are a witness for yourself
p: Jewish law did not accept a person's testimony about himself. Jesus agreed in 5:31 and now answers differently.
b: The Mishnah states the principle: "No one may testify about himself" (Ketubot 2:9). Jesus had granted it earlier: "If I give testimony about myself, my testimony does not hold true" (5:31), and then named other witnesses, John, his works, the Father and the Scriptures. Now he adds that his witness holds because he alone knows where he came from (8:14), and because the Father testifies with him (8:18), which makes the two witnesses the law requires (8:17).

a: You judge by the flesh
p: By human standards, by outward appearance. Jesus has just said to judge rightly (7:24).
b: Kata tēn sarka, "according to the flesh," means by ordinary human measures, outward and limited, like judging "by how things look" (7:24). John uses "flesh" for human life as weak and earthbound (1:13; 3:6; 6:63), though "the Word became flesh" (1:14). Jesus says he is not judging anyone, then that if he does, his judgment is true. Both are true in John: he came to save, not to condemn (3:17), yet his coming brings judgment on those who refuse the light (3:19; 9:39).
orig: κατὰ τὴν σάρκα (kata tēn sarka)

a: It is even written in your law
p: Jesus says "your law" here and in 10:34. Some hear distance; others hear "the law you yourselves accept."
b: The rule cited is Deuteronomy 19:15: "A matter is to stand on the word of two witnesses or on the word of three witnesses" (compare Deuteronomy 17:6). "Your law" (also 10:34; 15:25) sounds strange from a Jewish teacher who kept the festivals. Some scholars hear the voice of John's later community, which no longer felt at home in the synagogue. Others take it as an argument from the hearers' own premises: "the law you appeal to against me." Jesus still calls the Scripture unbreakable (10:35), so it is not a rejection of the law.

a: Where is your father?
p: They may simply misunderstand, or hint that Jesus' birth was suspect, as 8:41 may also hint. The Greek itself is a plain question.
b: Taken plainly, the hearers think of a human father and ask where he is, the kind of misunderstanding John uses often (3:4; 4:11). Some interpreters hear a taunt: in that culture a man was known by his father, and "Where is your father?" could hint at illegitimacy, a charge that 8:41 ("We are not the children of sexual sin") may echo. Jesus answers at the level of knowing God: to know him is to know the Father (14:7–9).

a: the treasury area
p: In the Court of Women, near the great lamps, stood thirteen chests for temple gifts.
b: The Mishnah describes thirteen trumpet-shaped collecting chests in the temple (Shekalim 6:5). They stood in the Court of Women, where Mark places the widow's two small coins (Mark 12:41–44) and where the great lamps of the festival were lit. So Jesus' "I am the light of the world" (8:12) was spoken next to the lampstands. The council chamber of the Sanhedrin, according to a later tradition, was not far off, which sharpens the note that no one seized him.

a: He isn't going to kill himself, is he?
p: A mocking guess that turns out to be half true: no one takes his life from him; he lays it down.
b: In 7:35 they guessed he would leave for the Greek world. Now they guess suicide, which most Jews of the time regarded as a grave sin; Josephus has himself argue that the souls of those who kill themselves go to the darker part of Hades (Jewish War 3.375). The guess is wrong but strangely close. Jesus will die by his own free choice: "No one takes it away from me. I lay it down by my own choice" (10:18). John's readers would feel the irony.

a: You belong to what is below
p: Two realms: this world, and the world of God. Jesus comes from above.
b: Literally "you are from the things below; I am from the things above." John often speaks in pairs like this: above and below, light and darkness, truth and lie, spirit and flesh. Some scholars once traced it to Greek or Gnostic thinking, but the Dead Sea Scrolls showed that Jews in Jesus' day used the same pairs, "sons of light" and "sons of darkness" (Community Rule 3–4). In John the pairs are not fixed fate: people from below can be born "from above" (3:3, 31).
orig: ὑμεῖς ἐκ τῶν κάτω ἐστέ, ἐγὼ ἐκ τῶν ἄνω εἰμί (hymeis ek tōn katō este, egō ek tōn anō eimi)

a: that I am
p: The Greek has no "he." It echoes how God speaks of himself in Isaiah.
b: Ean mē pisteusēte hoti egō eimi: "unless you believe that I am." Most English versions add "he" ("that I am he"), which is possible Greek. But the bare form matches the Greek of Isaiah 43:10, where God says, "so that you may know and believe ... that I am" (hoti egō eimi), and Deuteronomy 32:39, "I, only I, am he." Many scholars think John intends that echo, since it builds to 8:58. The question that follows, "Who are you?", shows the hearers caught the claim was unfinished. See the topic page on the "I am" sayings.
orig: ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ πιστεύσητε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι (ean gar mē pisteusēte hoti egō eimi)

a: Why am I even talking to you?
p: One of the hardest sentences in John. It can be a weary question or a claim about "the beginning."
b: The Greek, tēn archēn ho ti kai lalō hymin, can be read at least three ways. (1) As a question, "Why am I even talking to you?", taking tēn archēn as "at all," a sense known in Greek; this is the reading of several Greek fathers and the punctuation of the SBL text, which the Plain English Translation follows. (2) "What I have been telling you from the beginning" (KJV "Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning"), the reading of many English versions. (3) "I am the Beginning, which is what I am telling you," as the Latin Vulgate (principium) and some fathers took it. The first hand of Papyrus 66 adds "I told you," which supports reading (2), as Metzger and Comfort report (see the variant).
orig: Τὴν ἀρχὴν ὅ τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν (tēn archēn ho ti kai lalō hymin)

a: When you lift up the Son of Man
p: Hypsoō means both "raise up high" and "exalt." In John it points to the cross.
b: John uses hypsoō three times for the Son of Man: "Moses raised the snake high in the wilderness" (3:14), here, and "if I am lifted up from the earth" (12:32), which John explains as the kind of death he would die (12:33). The bronze snake on a pole (Numbers 21:8–9) is the picture: lifted up to be looked at and to give life. The verb also means "exalt," as in the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, where the servant "will be lifted up and glorified greatly." So the cross is Jesus' enthronement. The speakers "lift him up" by handing him over to be crucified, and in doing so make the "I am" visible.
orig: ὅταν ὑψώσητε τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (hotan hypsōsēte ton huion tou anthrōpou)

a: the Jews who had put their trust in him
t: Believers who want to kill him?
p: Jesus speaks to Jews who had believed, yet by 8:59 the audience picks up stones. How can that be?
b: Three main readings: (1) Their faith was real but shallow, and it broke when Jesus said they needed to be set free (D. A. Carson and many others). (2) The scene mirrors John's own day: Jewish believers in Jesus who would not break with the synagogue or accept the community's high claims about him, and whom the Gospel answers harshly (Raymond Brown and others). (3) The audience shifts: "they" in 8:33 are the wider crowd, not the new believers. Each reading affects how 8:44 is heard: on any of them, the words were spoken to people in a quarrel among Jews, not to the Jewish people as a whole.

a: the truth will make you free
p: Carved on many campuses and on the CIA's lobby wall, the saying in John is about knowing Jesus.
b: The verse is often quoted as a motto for learning or for openness in government; it is carved, for example, in the lobby of the CIA's original headquarters building. In John, though, "truth" is not information in general. It is God's reality made known in Jesus, who says, "I am the way, the truth and the life" (14:6), and the freedom is release from slavery to sin (8:34–36). The condition comes first: "If you remain in my word" (8:31). The motto use is fine as an echo, but it is not what the sentence means here.
orig: ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς (hē alētheia eleutherōsei hymas)

a: We have never been anyone's slaves
p: Israel had been slaves in Egypt and was ruled by Rome. They mean freedom of birth and spirit.
b: Israel's story begins in slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 26:5–8), and in Jesus' day Judea was under Rome. The speakers probably mean that, as Abraham's free-born heirs, they had never been slaves in their identity, whatever empire ruled. Josephus says the movement of Judas the Galilean in AD 6 held that God alone was their master (Antiquities 18.23). Jesus moves the question to a deeper slavery that birth cannot cure: sin.

a: The slave does not remain in the house for all time
t: Slave and son in the household
p: A slave could be sold or sent away; a son belongs to the house. Paul tells the same contrast through Hagar.
b: In an ancient household the slave (doulos) belonged to the family but had no right to stay or inherit. The son did. Israel's story had a famous case: Sarah said, "Throw out this slave woman and her son" (Genesis 21:10), and Ishmael was sent away while Isaac stayed. Paul uses the same story in Galatians 4:21–31. Jesus' point: descent from Abraham does not settle whether you are slave or son. The Son, who belongs to the house for all time, can free slaves and make them children (1:12).

a: do the things you heard from your father
p: It can mean "you do what you heard from your father" or "do what you heard from the Father." The Plain English Translation takes the first.
b: In the oldest text "the father" has no "your," and poieite can be a statement ("you do") or a command ("do!"). Read as a statement, the verse contrasts two fathers, and 8:41–44 then names theirs; this is how most interpreters and translations take it, and the Plain English Translation follows it, adding "your" to make the English clear. Read as a command, Jesus is still inviting them: "So you too must do what you heard from the Father" (Brown and some others prefer this). Later copyists settled it by adding "my" and "your" (see the variant), and the KJV follows them. The Plain English Translation chose the statement because the next verses turn at once to the question of whose children they are.
orig: καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν ἃ ἠκούσατε παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ποιεῖτε (kai hymeis oun ha ēkousate para tou patros poieite)

a: the works of Abraham
p: Abraham welcomed God's messengers. Children are known by acting like their father.
b: Jewish teachers also said that being Abraham's child meant sharing his character: "A good eye, a humble spirit and a modest soul: these are the disciples of Abraham our father" (Mishnah Avot 5:19). Abraham "put his trust in the LORD" (Genesis 15:6), and he ran to welcome the three visitors through whom the LORD appeared to him (Genesis 18:1–8). Jesus' complaint is that they want to kill the messenger who brings God's truth, "That is not something Abraham did" (8:40). Paul and James both argue about who Abraham's true children are (Romans 4; Galatians 3:7; James 2:21–23).
r: Genesis 15:6; Genesis 18:1–8; Romans 4:11–16; Galatians 3:7; James 2:21–23; Matthew 3:9

a: We are not the children of sexual sin
p: They may be hinting that Jesus was born of an affair, or claiming that Israel never served idols.
b: Porneia means sexual immorality, and the prophets used it for idolatry, Israel "playing the prostitute" with other gods (Hosea 1:2; 2:4). Read that way, the speakers say: we are not children of idolatry; God alone is our Father (Malachi 2:10). Many interpreters also hear a jab at Jesus, with "we" stressed: we were not born of fornication, as people say of you. The later rumor that Mary had a child by a soldier is reported by the pagan writer Celsus, who claimed it came from a Jew (Origen, Against Celsus 1.28, 32). If the jab is meant, it shows that Jesus' unusual birth was a point of argument early on.
r: Hosea 1:2; Hosea 2:4; Malachi 2:10; Isaiah 63:16; Matthew 1:18–25; Mark 6:3; 8:19

a: You come from your father, the devil
t: "Your father the devil": who heard it, and how it was misused
p: Spoken to particular opponents in a fierce dispute. Later Christians turned it against all Jews.
b: In the story the words are aimed at people who want to kill Jesus (8:37, 40), Jews arguing with a Jewish teacher in the temple. Harsh family language was common in disputes within Judaism: the prophets called Israel's leaders "offspring of an adulteress" (Isaiah 57:3), the Dead Sea Scrolls call fellow Jews "sons of darkness" and Belial's lot, and 1 John 3:8–10 says the same of Christians who hate their brothers. The Gospel's first readers, probably cut off from their synagogue, heard it in that heat. Later, Christians read it as a verdict on the Jewish people. Medieval preaching, Luther's On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) and Nazi propaganda all used it; Elvira Bauer's 1936 children's book Trust No Fox, printed by Julius Streicher's press, opens with the line "The father of the Jews is the devil." The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate (1965) and many Protestant bodies have rejected that reading. See the chapter page.

a: From the start he was a killer of people
p: Jesus points to Eden and to Cain: the devil's first lie led to death.
b: Anthrōpoktonos, "man-killer," points to the beginning. In Eden the snake's lie, "You will not die, not you!" (Genesis 3:4), brought death into the world, and a Jewish book of wisdom written before Jesus says, "through the devil's envy death entered the world" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24). The first murder followed when Cain killed his brother (Genesis 4:8), and 1 John 3:12 calls Cain "from the evil one." So Jesus links murder and lying: those who plan to kill him are doing the devil's first work.
orig: ἀνθρωποκτόνος ἦν ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς (anthrōpoktonos ēn ap' archēs)
r: Genesis 3:1–5; Genesis 4:8; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24; 1 John 3:8–15; Revelation 12:9

a: a Samaritan
p: A slur: Samaritans were seen as heretics and outsiders. Jesus denies the demon, not the Samaritan.
b: Samaritans worshiped the God of Israel on Mount Gerizim, kept only the five books of Moses, and were seen by Judeans as a half-foreign, heretical people (4:9). Calling a Jew a Samaritan meant he was disloyal and perhaps a sorcerer; Samaria was the home of Simon the magician (Acts 8:9–11). Jesus answers, "I have no demon," and lets the word "Samaritan" pass. Readers who remember chapter 4, where Samaritans call him "the Savior of the world" (4:42), may see why.

a: he will not see death, ever
p: Jesus speaks of the death that ends life with God, not of the body's death. His hearers take it literally.
b: "See death" and "taste death" (8:52) are Hebrew ways of saying "die." Jesus' hearers point out that Abraham and the prophets died. In John, eternal life begins now for the one who believes (5:24) and is not ended by the body's death: "Those who believe in me, even if they die, will live" (11:25). The misunderstanding is typical of John: people hear on one level, Jesus speaks on another.

a: Abraham your father was overjoyed that he would see my day
t: When did Abraham see Jesus' day?
p: Jewish traditions said God showed Abraham the future. John says what Abraham saw was Jesus' day.
b: Jewish interpreters taught that God showed Abraham the ages to come, at the covenant between the pieces (Genesis 15; Genesis Rabbah 44:22; 4 Ezra 3:14). Abraham "laughed" at the promise of Isaac (Genesis 17:17), which the Aramaic Targum Onqelos renders "rejoiced," and Jubilees 16 tells how Abraham kept the first Feast of Booths with great joy after Isaac's birth. Christians also thought of Mount Moriah: "God will see to the lamb for a burnt offering himself, my son" (Genesis 22:8). "My day" may mean Jesus' coming, his death and rising, or the final day. Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs saw the promises "from far away."
r: Genesis 15:5–21; Genesis 17:17; Genesis 22:8–14; Hebrews 11:13; Hebrews 11:17–19; Jubilees 16:20–31; 4 Ezra 3:14

a: You are not even fifty
p: A round number for a man not yet old. Irenaeus took it to mean Jesus was in his forties.
b: Fifty was the age when Levites retired from service (Numbers 4:3), the mark of a full working life. The hearers mean, "You are still a young man." Luke says Jesus was "about thirty" when he began (Luke 3:23). Irenaeus argued from this verse that Jesus taught into his forties, so that he passed through every age (Against Heresies 2.22.6), but most readers since have taken fifty as a round figure.

a: before Abraham came to be, I am
t: "Before Abraham came to be, I am"
p: Not "I was," but "I am": Abraham came into being, Jesus simply is. His hearers understood it as a claim to divinity.
b: Two verbs stand side by side. Abraham genesthai, "came into being," had a beginning. Jesus says egō eimi, "I am," present tense and with no predicate. Psalm 90:2 sets the same contrast for God: "Before the mountains were born ... you are God." The bare "I am" echoes God's words in the Greek of Isaiah (43:10–13; 46:4) and Exodus 3:14, where God names himself to Moses (in the Hebrew, "I will be who I will be"). The hearers pick up stones (8:59), the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). Jehovah's Witnesses translate "I have been" and read a claim to have existed before Abraham as a created spirit; see the card on this chapter's page.
orig: πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί (prin Abraam genesthai egō eimi)

a: Jesus was hidden
p: The verb can mean "he hid" or "he was hidden." Some see God's glory leaving the temple.
b: Ekrybē is passive in form: "he was hidden," perhaps by God, or simply "he hid himself." The next words, "he went out of the temple," close the long scene at the Feast of Booths that began in 7:14. Some interpreters see an echo of Ezekiel, where God's glory leaves the temple (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:22–23): the one who is "I am" walks out of his Father's house. Jesus hides again in 12:36 at the end of his public ministry. Later manuscripts add that he passed through the middle of them (see the variant).
orig: Ἰησοῦς δὲ ἐκρύβη (Iēsous de ekrybē)

a: whose sin caused him to be born blind
p: Many assumed illness came from sin. Later rabbis even asked whether a baby could sin before birth.
b: The law spoke of guilt passed to children of those who hate God (Exodus 20:5), and Job's friends argued that suffering proves sin. Ezekiel 18:20 had insisted that each person answers for his own wrong. The disciples' question allows two options: the man's own sin, which would have to be before birth, or his parents'. Later rabbis did discuss whether a child could sin in the womb, pointing to Jacob and Esau struggling before birth (Genesis Rabbah 63:6). Jesus rejects both options. Compare Luke 13:1–5, where he denies that victims of disaster were worse sinners.

a: it is so that God's works can be shown openly in him
t: "So that God's works": purpose or result?
p: Did God make him blind for this moment? The Greek allows another way to read it.
b: Read straight, the man was born blind "so that" God's works might be shown, which troubles many readers: did God cause decades of blindness for one miracle? Some answer that John speaks of God's purpose working through suffering, not causing it; the sentence does not say God made him blind. Others punctuate differently, since ancient Greek had none: Neither this man nor his parents sinned; but so that God's works may be shown in him, we must do the works of the one who sent me. Then the purpose clause goes with Jesus' work, not with the blindness.
orig: ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα φανερωθῇ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ (all' hina phanerōthē ta erga tou theou en autō)

a: he spat on the ground and made a paste of clay
p: Saliva was a known remedy in the ancient world. The clay also recalls God shaping Adam from the ground.
b: Pliny the Elder lists saliva among cures for eye trouble (Natural History 28.7), and Tacitus tells how the emperor Vespasian, in Alexandria, was begged to heal a blind man by spitting in his eyes (Histories 4.81). Jesus uses saliva also in Mark 7:33 and 8:23. Irenaeus saw more: the Word who formed the first human from the dust of the ground now forms new eyes from clay (Against Heresies 5.15.2; compare Genesis 2:7). Making clay also mattered legally: kneading is one of the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2), and John notes it was a Sabbath (9:14).

a: the pool of Siloam
p: A pool at the south end of Jerusalem, fed by Hezekiah's tunnel. Its remains were found in 2004.
b: Siloam (Hebrew Shiloach, "sent" or "channel") was fed by water carried from the Gihon spring through the tunnel cut under King Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30). In 2004 workers repairing a sewer pipe uncovered the steps of a large stepped pool of the Second Temple period at the south end of the City of David, excavated by Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron, now widely identified as John's pool. Water for the libation at the Feast of Booths was drawn from Siloam. John translates the name, "Sent," because Jesus is the one sent by the Father (9:4).

a: I am he
p: The healed man uses the same words, egō eimi, simply to say "It's me."
b: Here egō eimi means no more than "I am the one." That is useful for reading Jesus' sayings: the phrase is ordinary Greek, and only context gives it weight. When Jesus says it with no predicate after talking of Abraham, or when soldiers fall back at it (18:6), John means more. The healed man, who is learning who Jesus is, is the only other person in the Gospel who says "I am" this way.
orig: Ἐγώ εἰμι (egō eimi)

a: It was a Sabbath
p: Healing that was not urgent, and kneading clay, broke Sabbath rules as many teachers saw them.
b: Jewish law listed thirty-nine main kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath, including kneading (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). Saving a life overrode the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6), but this man had been blind from birth and could have waited a day. So some Pharisees reason by the law: a man who breaks the Sabbath cannot be from God (9:16). Others reason from the sign: a sinner could not do this. Both arguments were serious. The question was not whether to keep the Sabbath, but who has authority to say what keeping it means (5:17).

a: He is a prophet
t: The man sees more and more
p: His sight grows step by step. The Pharisees, who claim to see, slide the other way.
b: The healed man moves from "the man named Jesus" (9:11) to "a prophet" (9:17), to "from God" (9:33), to "I believe, Lord" and worship (9:38). His questioners move the opposite way: from division (9:16), to "this man is a sinner" (9:24), to "we do not know where he is from" (9:29), and finally to Jesus' verdict that their sin remains (9:41). John builds the chapter as a reversal, summed up in 9:39: the blind see, and those who see become blind.

a: The Jews, though, would not believe
p: Here "the Jews" are the same Pharisees who questioned the man in 9:13–17, not the Jewish people.
b: The scene began with "the Pharisees" (9:13–16), and now the same questioners are called "the Jews." The man and his parents are Jewish too, and the parents fear "the Jews" (9:22). So the word marks the religious authorities who hold power over the synagogue. John's switch from "Pharisees" to "the Jews" in one scene shows how the term works in this Gospel: it names a group of opponents in the story, and most scholars think it reflects the conflict of John's own day, when believers in Jesus were being put out of synagogues. See the notes at 7:1 and 9:22.

a: thrown out of the synagogue
p: Was there a formal ban on believers in Jesus? This verse is at the center of a long scholarly debate.
b: Aposynagōgos, "away from the synagogue," appears only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). J. Louis Martyn argued in 1968 that chapter 9 tells two stories at once: Jesus' day and John's own day, when a curse on heretics in the synagogue prayers, the Birkat ha-Minim (said to be revised under Gamaliel II at Yavneh, about AD 85), drove Jewish Christians out. This view shaped decades of scholarship. Critics, among them Reuven Kimelman, Daniel Boyarin and Adele Reinhartz, answer that there is no evidence of a single decree aimed at Christians in the first century; the earliest texts of the prayer are much later. Many scholars now think of local expulsions (compare Luke 6:22; 2 Corinthians 11:24), and some read the verse as Jesus' own time described in the language of later conflict.

a: Give God the glory!
p: An oath formula: "Tell the truth before God and confess." Joshua said it to Achan.
b: When Achan was caught, Joshua said, "My son, please give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make your confession to him" (Joshua 7:19). So the phrase means "Swear before God to tell the truth," and it carries a hint: "confess that you have been lying." The leaders want the man to admit a fraud, or at least to give God the credit and not Jesus. With deep irony, the man does give glory to God by telling the truth about Jesus.

a: We are disciples of Moses
p: The Pharisees present themselves as heirs of Moses. John presents Jesus as the one Moses wrote about.
b: The Pharisees and the rabbis after them saw themselves as links in a chain going back to Moses: "Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it on to Joshua" (Mishnah Avot 1:1), and Jesus once said scribes and Pharisees "sit in Moses' seat" (Matthew 23:2). For them, loyalty to Moses ruled out following a Sabbath-breaker. John sees no such choice: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me too, because it was about me that he wrote" (5:46). The split in this verse is the split John's readers lived through.

a: We know that God does not listen to sinners
p: The man quotes a common biblical idea to argue with his questioners. It is his argument, not a rule about prayer.
b: The idea runs through the Old Testament: "If I had looked with favor on evil in my heart, the Lord would not listen" (Psalm 66:18; compare Isaiah 1:15; Proverbs 15:29; Job 27:9). The man uses it against the leaders' own logic: if Jesus were a sinner, God would not have answered him. Some Christians have taken the verse alone to teach that God never hears the prayer of an unbeliever, but elsewhere God hears sinners who cry out in repentance (Luke 18:13–14), and the man is arguing, not laying down doctrine.
r: Psalm 66:18; Psalm 34:15; Isaiah 1:15; Proverbs 15:29; Job 27:9; Luke 18:13–14; 1 John 5:14

a: not a single report has been heard of someone opening the eyes of a person born blind
p: The Old Testament has no healing of someone born blind. The prophets saved it for the age to come.
b: Elisha prayed and the LORD opened the eyes of soldiers he had struck blind (2 Kings 6:18–20), and Tobit was healed of blindness caused by bird droppings (Tobit 11:10–13), but no story tells of eyes blind from birth being opened. Isaiah promised it for God's coming salvation: "Then blind people's eyes will open" (Isaiah 35:5; compare Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 42:7). Opening blind eyes is a sign that the new age has come (Matthew 11:5). The man's argument is strong for his hearers.
r: Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 35:5; Isaiah 42:7; Psalm 146:8; 2 Kings 6:18–20; Tobit 11:10–13; Matthew 11:5

a: bowed down and worshiped him
p: Proskyneō means to bow low, to kneel in homage. In John it is the word for worshiping God.
b: Proskyneō was used for bowing before kings as well as for worshiping God, so it can mean homage. But in John it appears elsewhere only for worshiping God, ten times in the talk with the Samaritan woman about worship "in spirit and truth" (4:20–24), and once for Greeks coming to worship at the festival (12:20). This is the only place in John where someone bows in worship before Jesus. Some early manuscripts lack this verse; see the variant.
orig: προσεκύνησεν αὐτῷ (prosekynēsen autō)

a: I came into this world to bring judgment
p: Jesus came to save, not to condemn (3:17), yet his light divides people. Isaiah 6 lies behind this.
b: In 3:17 Jesus did not come "to judge the world"; here he came "for judgment." Both are true: the light comes to save, but its coming exposes who loves darkness (3:19). The saying echoes Isaiah's call to make the people's eyes blind (Isaiah 6:9–10), which John quotes at the end of Jesus' public ministry (12:39–41), and Isaiah's promise that the blind will see (Isaiah 29:18; 42:16–19). The Pharisees' question shows they heard it as aimed at them.

a: the sheep's courtyard
p: A walled yard with one door, where sheep were kept at night. The same word is used for the temple courts.
b: Aulē is a courtyard, here an enclosure of stone walls, often beside a house, where one or more flocks spent the night with a doorkeeper on watch (10:3). The shepherd came in the morning, called his own sheep out, and led them to pasture. The word is also used for the temple's courtyards, and Jesus has just been in them; some interpreters hear a hint that the "fold" is Israel gathered around the temple, from which Jesus leads his sheep out (10:3–4, 16). The speech continues the scene with the Pharisees at the end of chapter 9, without a break.

a: a thief and a bandit
t: Who are the thieves and bandits?
p: Lēstēs is a bandit or armed rebel. Readers have named false leaders, false messiahs and the rulers of chapter 9.
b: Kleptēs is a sneak thief; lēstēs is a robber who uses force, the word Josephus uses for armed rebels and that John uses for Barabbas (18:40). Candidates include: the leaders who have just thrown out the healed man (9:34), Israel's bad shepherds condemned in Ezekiel 34; would-be messiahs and rebel leaders who promised freedom and led followers to death, as Josephus describes (compare Acts 5:36–37); or anyone who claims the flock without coming "through the door." The text does not settle it, and the picture fits all of them.

a: He calls out to his own sheep, each by name, and leads them outside
p: The good leader of Israel is one who leads the people out and brings them in.
b: Moses asked God for a leader "who will lead them out and bring them in, so that the LORD's community will not be like sheep with no one to shepherd them" (Numbers 27:17), and Joshua was given. God calls Israel by name: "I called you by your name. You belong to me" (Isaiah 43:1). Travelers and shepherds in the region have long described flocks that answer only their own shepherd's call, even when several flocks share a fold. The verb "leads out" (exagō) is the verb used for God leading Israel out of Egypt.

a: word picture
p: Paroimia means a proverb, figure of speech or riddle. John has no parables in the Synoptic sense.
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke use parabolē, "parable"; John never does. He uses paroimia, a veiled saying, a figure or riddle, here and in 16:25, 29, where Jesus promises to speak plainly at last. The shepherd image has several parts that Jesus then explains in turn: he is the door (10:7–10) and he is the shepherd (10:11–18). Mixing the images was normal in Jewish teaching, which used the shepherd figure for God, Moses, David and Israel's leaders.
orig: παροιμία (paroimia)

a: I am the door for the sheep
p: The way into the fold and out to pasture. Shepherds sometimes slept across the opening.
b: "This is the gate that belongs to the LORD; through it the righteous will enter" (Psalm 118:20). Jesus calls himself the door through which the sheep enter safety and go out to pasture (10:9). Writers on Middle Eastern shepherding have described shepherds lying across the opening of an open fold at night, so that the shepherd himself is the door; the description is often repeated, though how old the custom is cannot be checked. The saying anticipates 14:6: no one comes to the Father except through Jesus. One early papyrus reads "the shepherd of the sheep" here; see the variant.

a: Whoever goes in through me will be rescued
p: Sōzō means rescue, keep safe, heal, and save in the full religious sense. For sheep it means safe from harm.
b: Sōthēsetai, "will be saved," works on two levels. For a sheep, it means being safe from thieves and wolves. In John's larger sense it means being rescued for eternal life (3:17; 5:34). "Come in and go out" is a Hebrew way of describing a whole, free life (Deuteronomy 28:6; Numbers 27:17), and "pasture" recalls the shepherd of Psalm 23: "In meadows of fresh grass he has me lie down" (Psalm 23:2) and Ezekiel 34:14, "I will lead them out to good pasture."
orig: σωθήσεται (sōthēsetai), 'will be saved, kept safe'

a: have more than enough
p: Perisson means more than needed. In John the overflow is the life of God, not money or comfort.
b: Perisson echōsin, "have abundance, have more than enough." The verse is popular in teaching that God wants believers to be wealthy and healthy. In context, though, the "life" is the eternal life Jesus gives through his own death (10:11, 28), and the contrast is with a thief who kills. The overflow matches other signs in John: wine far beyond need at Cana (2:6–10) and twelve baskets of leftovers (6:12–13).
orig: ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχωσιν καὶ περισσὸν ἔχωσιν (hina zōēn echōsin kai perisson echōsin)

a: I am the good shepherd
p: Kalos means good in the sense of fine, noble, the shepherd as he should be. Israel's God was its shepherd.
b: Ho poimēn ho kalos is "the good shepherd" in the sense of the model, the true and noble one, as opposed to the hired man (10:12). Ancient kings called themselves shepherds; Hammurabi did in the prologue to his laws. Israel sang, "The LORD is my shepherd" (Psalm 23:1), and Ezekiel 34 condemned Israel's leaders as shepherds who fed themselves, then promised: "I myself will search for my sheep" and "I will set over them one shepherd, my servant David" (Ezekiel 34:11, 23). Jesus claims both roles at once: God's own shepherding and the promised David.
orig: ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός (ho poimēn ho kalos)
r: Psalm 23:1–4; Psalm 80:1; Ezekiel 34:1–31; Jeremiah 23:1–6; Isaiah 40:11; Zechariah 11:4–17; Hebrews 13:20; 1 Peter 5:4

a: lays down his own life for the sheep
p: A phrase found only in John's writings. Real shepherds risked their lives for their flocks.
b: Tēn psychēn tithēmi, "to lay down the life," appears in the New Testament only in John and 1 John (10:15, 17, 18; 13:37–38; 15:13; 1 John 3:16). It means giving one's life deliberately, as one sets down a garment (compare 13:4, where the same verb is used for Jesus laying aside his clothes). Shepherding was dangerous: David told Saul, "Your servant used to shepherd sheep for his father," and fought off lions and bears (1 Samuel 17:34–35). "For the sheep" (hyper) means on their behalf, in their place.
orig: τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ τίθησιν ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων (tēn psychēn autou tithēsin hyper tōn probatōn)

a: The hired man
p: A worker paid by the day, with no stake in the flock. The prophets denounced leaders like him.
b: The misthōtos works for wages. The law freed a keeper from paying for an animal torn by a wild beast (Exodus 22:10–13), but the Mishnah, applying this to a paid keeper, says that "one wolf is not an unavoidable accident; two wolves are" (Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:9). A hired shepherd was expected to stand against a single wolf. So Jesus' hired man runs even when he should stay. The prophets condemned Israel's leaders as shepherds who cared for themselves and let the flock be scattered (Ezekiel 34:2–6; Zechariah 11:16–17). The picture does not need one target; it describes any leader for whom the flock is a job.

a: I also have other sheep
p: Most readers say Gentiles; Latter-day Saints and Jehovah's Witnesses give other answers. See the chapter card.
b: The "other sheep" are "not of this courtyard," outside the fold of Israel. Most Christian readers, ancient and modern, take them to be Gentiles who would believe, since John later says Jesus would die "and not just for the nation. He would die to bring God's scattered children together into one" (11:52), and Greeks come seeking him (12:20–23). Some scholars think of scattered Jews or of separated Christian groups in John's day. Latter-day Saints read the verse with the Book of Mormon, where the risen Jesus tells people in the Americas that they are the other sheep (3 Nephi 15:21). Jehovah's Witnesses identify them as believers with an earthly hope, distinct from the 144,000 "little flock."

a: one flock with one shepherd
p: The KJV says "one fold," following the Latin. The Greek says one flock, a people, not one enclosure.
b: Jesus has just used aulē, "fold, courtyard" ("not of this fold"), and now says mia poimnē, "one flock." Jerome's Latin Vulgate used ovile, "sheepfold," for both, and the KJV followed it: "there shall be one fold, and one shepherd." The difference became a point of argument: "one fold" was cited for one visible church structure, while "one flock" stresses a people united by one shepherd. Ezekiel 34:23 and 37:24 promise "one shepherd" over a reunited Israel.
orig: μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν (mia poimnē, heis poimēn)

a: I have the right to lay it down, and I have the right to take it back again
p: Exousia means authority or right. Jesus claims power to give his life and to take it back.
b: Exousia is authority, the right and power to act. Elsewhere the New Testament usually says God raised Jesus (Acts 2:24; Romans 6:4), but John also has Jesus say, "Tear this temple down, and within three days I will raise it" (2:19). Christians have seen both as true, since the Son acts with the Father (5:19–21). The point for the first hearers is that Jesus' death would not be a defeat: "No one takes it away from me."
orig: ἐξουσίαν ἔχω (exousian echō)

a: He has a demon, and he is out of his mind
p: The same charges were made against Jesus in Mark, and earlier in this Gospel.
b: The accusation repeats 7:20 and 8:48, 52. In Mark 3:21–22 Jesus' family thinks he is out of his mind and scribes say he has a demon. The division of opinion, with some appealing to the healed blind man (10:21), shows that the debate of chapter 9 is still going on.

a: The Feast of Dedication
p: The eight-day festival remembering the cleansing of the temple in 164 BC, after the Syrian king defiled it.
b: In 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple. After the Maccabean revolt, Judas Maccabeus cleansed and rededicated the temple on 25 Kislev, 164 BC, and the people kept eight days of celebration (1 Maccabees 4:36–59; 2 Maccabees 10:1–8). Josephus calls the festival "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325). Enkainia, "renewal, dedication," is the Greek for Hebrew Hanukkah. It falls in December, "wintertime." At a festival celebrating a temple made holy again, Jesus speaks of himself as the one the Father "made holy and sent" (10:36). This is the only mention of Hanukkah in the New Testament, and in the Protestant Bible; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles also tell its origin in 1 and 2 Maccabees.

a: Solomon's Porch
p: A covered colonnade along the east side of the temple courts, sheltered from the winter wind.
b: Josephus describes a portico on the east side of the temple, which people believed went back to Solomon (Antiquities 20.221; Jewish War 5.185). In winter it gave shelter from the cold east wind. The early church met there (Acts 3:11; 5:12). John's note about winter and the porch is one of many small details that suggest he knew Jerusalem well.

a: How long are you going to leave us hanging?
t: "How long will you lift up our soul?"
p: A Greek idiom: keep us in suspense. It can also mean "annoy us," and some hear both.
b: Literally "Until when do you lift our soul?" The usual sense is "keep us in suspense" (compare the hearers' demand to speak plainly). In later Greek the same phrase meant "annoy, torment," and some scholars think the hearers say both: "How long will you torment us?" Jesus' reply, "I told you," points back to all he has said and done, though he has not used the word "Messiah" publicly in John; he said it privately to the Samaritan woman (4:26).
orig: Ἕως πότε τὴν ψυχὴν ἡμῶν αἴρεις; (heōs pote tēn psychēn hēmōn aireis)

a: The Jews surrounded him
p: In 10:24–39, "the Jews" are the temple audience who press Jesus and then pick up stones: leaders and their supporters.
b: The same word comes three times in this scene: those who surround Jesus (10:24), who lift stones (10:31), and who accuse him of blasphemy (10:33). Just before, "the Jews" were divided, some defending Jesus (10:19–21), and afterward many believe (10:42; 11:45). So the word cannot mean the whole people, who are on both sides. It names a hostile group in the temple, most likely led by the authorities who had already tried to arrest him (7:32; 8:59). See the note at 7:1.

a: since you do not belong among my sheep
p: Do people believe because they are sheep, or become sheep by believing? Churches read this differently.
b: Jesus says they do not believe because they are not his sheep, which seems to put belonging first and believing second. Reformed readers see here God's choosing: the Father gives sheep to the Son (6:37, 44; 10:29), and they then believe. Wesleyan and other readers note that the same chapter invites the hearers to believe the works (10:38), so their not being sheep describes a refusal they could still turn from, as some did (10:42; 11:45). See the card on this chapter's page.

a: nobody will snatch them from my hand
p: Jesus uses for himself the claim God makes in the Song of Moses: no one can pull anyone out of my hand.
b: In Deuteronomy God says, "I kill, and I make alive ... and no one can pull anyone out of my hand" (Deuteronomy 32:39), and in Isaiah, "No one can rescue anyone from my hand" (Isaiah 43:13). Jesus says it of his own hand (10:28) and then of the Father's (10:29), which prepares for 10:30. Christians have drawn from these verses the comfort that believers are safe; whether a believer can walk away on his own is a separate debate; see the chapter card.

a: I and the Father are one
p: The Greek hen is neuter, "one thing," not "one person." Early theologians used both halves of the verse.
b: Jesus does not say heis, "one person," but hen, "one thing, one reality." Augustine pointed out that the verse answers two errors: "one" against those who made the Son less than the Father, and "are" (plural) against those who said Father and Son are the same person (Tractates on John 36.9). Some readers, including Jehovah's Witnesses and many Latter-day Saints, take it as unity of will and purpose, as in 17:21–22, "so that they may be one as we are one." The hearers took it as more (10:33). Richard Bauckham hears an echo of the Shema, "The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4): Jesus is included in the one God.
orig: ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν (egō kai ho patēr hen esmen)

a: because you, a human being, are making yourself God
p: To claim to be equal with God was blasphemy, which the law punished by stoning.
b: "Whoever speaks the name of the LORD with contempt must be put to death. The whole community must stone him" (Leviticus 24:16). The Mishnah later narrowed the crime to pronouncing the divine name itself (Sanhedrin 7:5), but in Jesus' day the charge could cover any claim that insulted God's honor. The accusation, "you, a human being, are making yourself God," restates 5:18 and is John's own claim turned upside down: in the prologue the Word, who was God, became flesh (1:1, 14).

a: 'I said, You are gods'
p: Jesus quotes Psalm 82. Who the "gods" are in the psalm is itself debated.
b: Psalm 82 says, "I said, 'You are gods, and sons of the Most High, every one of you'" (Psalm 82:6). Readers identify these "gods" as: (1) Israel's judges, who held God's authority to judge (compare Exodus 21:6, where "to God" may mean "to the judges"); (2) Israel at Sinai, who received God's word, as some rabbis taught (Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 5a), which fits "the people the word of God came to" (10:35); (3) heavenly beings in God's council, the view of many scholars of the Psalms today (Psalm 82:1). Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture can call them gods, he is not blaspheming to call himself God's Son. "Your law" here means Scripture as a whole, since the verse is from the Psalms.

a: the Scripture cannot be undone
p: Lyō means loosen, break, annul. Jesus treats even one phrase of a psalm as binding.
b: Ou dynatai lythēnai hē graphē: Scripture "cannot be loosed," cannot be set aside or made void. The same verb is used for "breaking" the Sabbath or the law (5:18; 7:23). Jesus' argument rests on a single word, "gods," in a single psalm. Christians who hold that Scripture is without error, such as B. B. Warfield, have often appealed to this verse. Others note that it is an argument from the hearers' shared premise, and that it speaks of Scripture's authority more than of a theory of how it was written. Both groups agree that Jesus treats Scripture as God's binding word.
orig: οὐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφή (ou dynatai lythēnai hē graphē)

a: the one the Father made holy and sent into the world
t: Made holy at the festival of making holy
p: At Hanukkah, the festival of the temple made holy again, Jesus calls himself the one the Father made holy.
b: Hēgiasen, "made holy, consecrated, set apart," is the language of dedicating an altar or a temple (Numbers 7:1; 1 Maccabees 4:48). Spoken at the Feast of Dedication (10:22), it suggests that Jesus is the true holy place, consecrated by God himself, as John said of his body as the temple (2:21). Jeremiah was also "made holy" before birth for his mission (Jeremiah 1:5), and in 17:17–19 Jesus asks the Father to make his disciples holy.

a: to the place where John had been baptizing in the early days
p: Jesus' public ministry ends where it began, at John's baptizing place beyond the Jordan.
b: "Bethany beyond the Jordan," where John testified about Jesus (1:28), frames the public ministry: it starts there and, after a last visit to Jerusalem at Hanukkah, Jesus withdraws there. The place may have been near Jericho, on the east bank. The next scene, the raising of Lazarus, calls him back across the river to Bethany near Jerusalem (11:1–7).

a: John did not do a single sign
p: No Gospel credits John the Baptist with miracles. His work was to testify.
b: John the Baptist worked no miracles in any of the Gospels, and Josephus remembers him as a good man who called Jews to righteousness and baptism, not as a wonder-worker (Antiquities 18.116–119). The crowd's verdict is the Fourth Gospel's verdict on him: his testimony was true (1:7–8, 15, 29–34; 5:33). It may also answer followers of John who ranked him above Jesus (compare Acts 19:1–7).
